title: Teaching
text:
I teach students to think scientifically, evaluate evidence critically, and become increasingly independent learners. My courses combine structured practice, active learning, and scaffolded projects so that students can build difficult skills before using them independently.
Whether or not students continue in psychology, I want them to leave my courses better able to ask good questions, evaluate claims, communicate evidence, and solve problems.

title: Teaching
text:
How I Teach

Build Independence Through Scaffolding
The PSY 250 research proposal is my clearest example. Students begin by evaluating a springboard article and searching the literature, then develop a research question, hypotheses, and variables. Through outlines, peer review, and instructor feedback, they build individual components before integrating them into a complete research proposal and presentation.


Teach Students to Trace Claims Back to Evidence
In one activity, students locate popular articles that make claims about detox diets, identify the scientific sources those articles cite, find the original research, and compare what the evidence supports with how the claim is presented publicly. The exercise turns scientific literacy into a concrete habit: follow a claim back to its evidence before deciding what to believe.


Learn Actively
I use think-pair-share, small-group discussion, student-generated examples, and applied research-design activities to give students repeated opportunities to practice reasoning rather than only listen to explanations. These activities ask students to explain concepts, evaluate evidence, make methodological decisions, and learn from how their classmates approach the same problem.


Connect Learning to Transferable Skills
Students practice critical thinking, project management, communication, teamwork, public speaking, and evidence evaluation throughout my courses. These skills remain useful whether students continue in psychology, pursue another field, or apply what they have learned outside the classroom.

title: Mentoring
text:
I want research assistants to leave the lab with more than completed hours. Their experience should build research skills, confidence, career clarity, and increasing independence. Because students join research teams for different reasons, I tailor opportunities to their goals rather than assuming that every student wants an academic career.
Students interested in research-intensive careers may progress toward literature review, analysis, conference presentations, and manuscript writing, while others may emphasize communication, teamwork, project management, participant interaction, and scientific literacy.

title: Mentoring
text:
From Training to Independence
I tailor students’ research experiences to their goals, interests, and level of experience. Early conversations about why they joined the lab, what skills they want to develop, and what they hope to do next help us identify responsibilities and opportunities that fit their goals. From there, my mentoring follows a developmental progression: students begin with clear structure, gain autonomy as their skills grow, and can eventually take on leadership and ownership within the research team.

Start with Structure
New research assistants begin with detailed written protocols, mock sessions, research-ethics guidance, clear expectations for documentation and reliability, competency checks, and close feedback. This structure gives students a dependable foundation for learning while protecting the quality of the research.
Example training resource:
SWaT Research Assistant Onboarding & Training Plan


Build Independence
As students gain experience, the goal shifts from simply following procedures to understanding why those procedures matter. Students learn to troubleshoot problems, connect day-to-day research tasks with study design and data quality, and make increasingly independent decisions within their roles.


Create Leadership Opportunities
Advanced students may take on roles in project coordination, recruitment, data quality, peer training, science communication, or project leadership. These roles give experienced students opportunities to mentor peers, improve workflows, monitor research quality, and take ownership of meaningful parts of a project.

title: Mentoring
section: Weekly Lab Meetings as a Research Seminar
text:
Weekly Lab Meetings as a Research Seminar
Weekly lab meetings function as a research seminar rather than only an operations meeting. We discuss assigned papers, student-generated questions, study design, methods, data-quality issues, conference presentations, and manuscripts. I also use short methods lessons and applied exercises to expose students to research skills they may not encounter in their coursework.
For example, students might code a short interview excerpt while learning about qualitative methods or use a meta-analysis paper to discuss how researchers synthesize evidence across studies.

title: Mentoring
text:
Learning the Research Lifecycle
Students may enter a project during recruitment or data collection, but I want them to understand how research develops from an idea into a study, dataset, conference presentation, and publication. Depending on their interests and time in the lab, students may contribute to literature review, protocol development, recruitment, data collection, quality control, analysis, dissemination, or writing.
Mentee trajectory: One of my undergraduate research mentees began on my team running study sessions and later contributed to literature review, study planning, project coordination, conference presentations, and manuscript writing. Our mentoring relationship continued after she left CSU and during her time at Brown University as a full-time research coordinator, and she is now pursuing a Ph.D. in Clinical Psychology.

Across 67 mentoring evaluations collected from 2022–2026, students rated their overall research experience an average of 4.79/5; among those completing the mentor-specific item, my average overall mentor rating was 4.92/5.

“I have learned so much being in this lab. I felt like I was able to grow a lot personally and academically. The article presentations allowed me to practice my public speaking skills and answering questions on the spot used to be an uncomfortable task for me but now I feel more at ease doing so. Skylar has been very patient and helpful throughout my whole experience as an RA and I am so grateful for this experience. I have never taken a research class or anything beyond Psych 100 so I have taken away alot of information from the field of psychology in this lab and am very proud to be part of it.”


“Overall, I absolutely loved this experience. I’ve learned so much from Skylar and offers incredible support and feedback. Her genuine interest in the research is infectious and makes me want to pursue academia.”


“This research experience exceeded my expectations. I went into this just thinking it would be something nice to throw onto my resume while giving me the chance to study a topic I’d never really put much consideration into. Now, I feel like I’ve learned so much about research as a whole and the topic of active workstations, and I truly had a good time with running the experiments, interacting with fellow RAs, and working with and hearing new ideas from Skylar. It has genuinely been such a pleasure to be a part of this study!”

Students also frequently describe gaining experience with study design, protocol administration, participant interaction, literature searching, data collection, research ethics, troubleshooting, and scientific communication.

title: Research
text:
My research asks how health-promoting behaviors can fit into people’s everyday lives rather than compete with them. I focus primarily on physical activity and sedentary behavior, studying how timing, task demands, individual differences, and everyday context shape whether an intervention is usable and effective.
Across this work, I return to one question: When, for whom, and under what conditions does an intervention work?


I study how light physical activity can be integrated into desk-based work and other everyday settings without disrupting performance or making everyday tasks harder.



The same intervention can help one person, burden another, and make little difference for someone else. I study how individual characteristics, task demands, timing, and context shape those differences.



I am interested in what happens after an intervention initially works: whether people keep using it, what helps healthy behavior become part of a routine, and how sustained behavior affects health and well-being.

title: Research
text:
From Laboratory to Everyday Life
I use controlled laboratory studies to isolate mechanisms and test causal questions, then field and mixed-methods studies to understand whether the same ideas remain useful in everyday settings.
The questions move in both directions. Practical barriers observed in the field inform new laboratory studies, while laboratory findings help identify what should be tested at larger scale.
Mechanism → Feasibility → Field effectiveness → Sustained use → Refined mechanism
This iterative approach lets practical constraints become part of the science rather than a problem discovered only after an intervention leaves the laboratory.

title: Research
text:
Representative Projects


Activity-Permissive Workstations, Performance, and User Experience
Can people walk while working without compromising the work itself? In a randomized study comparing sitting, standing, and treadmill walking, cognitive performance was similar across workstation conditions, although walking participants perceived typing and mouse use as more difficult. They also reported greater enjoyment and less boredom. The findings suggest that the usefulness of treadmill desks depends more on the task than on a simple “good versus bad” judgment.



Walking While Working Under Stress
Does walking remain workable when work becomes stressful and cognitively demanding? In a preregistered experiment, walking during an acute social-evaluative stressor did not buffer stress responses, but it also did not amplify perceived stress or workload. Walking participants rated the workstation as more enjoyable than sitting and more comfortable than standing. This work also shows why physiological responses during active work need to be interpreted against a movement-specific baseline.







Dissertation: When Should We Walk Around Stress?
My dissertation tests whether a brief walk works differently when it occurs before, during, or after an acute stressor. Preliminary quantitative findings do not suggest one universally optimal timing, while participants’ qualitative accounts reveal substantial differences in whether walking feels like preparation, coping, distraction, added demand, or recovery. I am using those differences to study how intervention timing and individual experience shape intervention fit.






Task-Specific Treadmill-Desk Feasibility
Not every office task is equally compatible with walking. This mixed-methods project examines which everyday tasks people are willing and able to complete on a treadmill desk, and how task demands, ergonomics, pace, social context, and user control shape that experience.


Longitudinal Treadmill-Desk Field Pilot
What determines whether someone continues using a treadmill desk once the novelty wears off? This year-long daily-diary pilot follows self-directed treadmill-desk use among administrative staff, examining use patterns, barriers, perceived benefits, and day-to-day context. The project is informing larger longitudinal studies of sustained movement at work.



Health Literacy and Menu Labeling
A complementary line of my research examines whether health information works equally well for different people. In a national sample of U.S. adults, I found substantial sociodemographic differences in functional health literacy. In a randomized menu-labeling study, nutrition labels were associated with healthier ordering primarily among adults with moderate health literacy rather than uniformly across literacy groups. Together, this work reinforces a broader theme of my research: population-level interventions can produce uneven effects depending on how well they fit the people expected to use them.

title: Research
text:
Methodological Approach
I use experiments, mixed methods, psychophysiology, qualitative interviews, and intensive longitudinal field designs. I choose methods around the question, often combining controlled tests of causal mechanisms with measures of feasibility, individual differences, and real-world use.

title: Research
text:
Where This Work Is Going
My next studies will extend this program from short-term feasibility toward sustained behavior change in everyday settings. I am particularly interested in comparing different ways of integrating movement into work, identifying person-by-context differences in response, and using repeated-measures and wearable-supported field studies to understand when healthy behavior becomes sustainable.
More broadly, I want to develop health interventions that fit people’s existing lives rather than requiring people to reorganize their lives around the intervention.
